questions.question: According to the Output Method, GDP is calculated as:

options.text: GDP at Constant Prices - Taxes + Subsidies
GDP at Constant Prices + Taxes - Subsidies

questions.solution:
The correct answer is__** GDP at Constant Prices - Taxes + Subsidies.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• According to the Output Method, GDP is calculated as GDP at Constant Prices - Taxes + Subsidies.__
 
• The **GDP Output Method measures** the monetary or market value of all the goods and services produced within the borders of the country.
 
• In order to avoid a distorted measure of GDP due to price level changes, GDP at constant prices or Real GDP is computed.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• GDP is the final value of the final goods and services produced within the geographic boundaries of a country during a specified period of time, normally a year.
 
• It counts the goods and services produced within the country and hence does not consider the products that the country imports from another country.
 
• **GDP calculation through income approach**:
 
 
• The GDP income approach formula starts with the income earned from the production of goods and services.
 
• GDP=Total National Income +Sales Taxes+Depreciation +Net Foreign Factor Income.
 
 
 
• **GDP calculation through Expenditure method:**
 
 
• ​This measures the total expenditure incurred by all entities on goods and services within the domestic boundaries of a country.
 
• GDP= Consumption expenditure + Investment expenditure + Government expenditure + (Exports - Imports).

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT included in domestic income?

options.text: Income earned by the residents of the country
Income earned by the non-residents outside the country
Income earned by all the employees of the country
Profit of all the industries of the country

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Income earned by the non-residents outside the country**__. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Domestic income, also known as Gross Domestic Product, is the total income earned by all sectors (households, firms, and the government) within the geographical boundaries of a country, irrespective of whether they are residents or non-residents.
 
• However, income earned by non-residents outside the country is NOT included in the domestic income. Such income is part of the national income, not domestic income.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)**: This is the total monetary value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders over a specific period, typically a year.
 
• **Gross National Product (GNP)**: It is the total market value of all final goods and services produced by residents of a country in a given period of time.
 
 
• **GNP = GDP + Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA)**
 
• Here, **Net Factor Income from Abroad = Income earned by domestic factors of production from rest of the world - Income earned by factors of production of rest of the world from the domestic economy**
 
 
 
• **Net National Product (NNP) at Factor Cost or National Income (NI)**: This is the GNP minus depreciation.
 
 
• NNP or NI = GNP - Depreciation
 
 
 
• **Net Domestic Product (NDP)**: This is the GDP minus depreciation.
 
 
• NDP = GDP - Depreciation
 
 
 
• **Per Capita Income**: It is a measure of the amount of money earned per person in a certain area.
 
 
• Per Capita Income = National Income / Total Population
 
 
 
• **Factor Income**: It's the income that factors of production (land, labour, capital, and entrepreneurship) receive in return for their contribution to the production process.
 
• **Transfer Payments:** These are payments made without the provision of goods or services in return. Examples are social security benefits, pensions, unemployment benefits, etc. Transfer payments are not included in the computation of national income as they do not involve productive activity.

questions.question: Which of the following types of direct tax collection increased as of 10 February 2023 budget?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Personal income tax is a type of direct tax levied by the government on the income of individuals and entities.
 
• The collection of personal income tax saw an increase as per the 10 February 2023 budget.
 
• This increase can be attributed to various economic factors such as higher earnings, improved compliance, and broader tax base.
 
• Personal income tax forms a significant portion of the revenue collected by the government, which is used for public welfare and development projects.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Personal Income Tax**

 
 
• It is a direct tax that individuals or entities pay on their income to the government.
 
• Income tax rates and slabs are determined by the government and can vary based on the amount of income earned.
 
• In most countries, including India, individuals are required to file an annual income tax return detailing their earnings and taxes due.
 
• Personal income tax is used by the government to fund various public services and infrastructure projects.
 
 
 
• **Octroi Duties**
 
 
• Octroi is a local tax collected on various goods entering a municipality or any specific area.
 
• It was a common form of taxation in India but has largely been abolished and replaced by other forms of indirect taxation.
 
 
 
• **Corporate Tax**
 
 
• Corporate tax is a direct tax imposed on the net income or profit of corporations and other business entities.
 
• The tax rate for corporations is usually different from that for individuals.
 
• Corporate tax is a significant source of revenue for the government.
 
 
 
• **Commercial Tax**
 
 
• Commercial tax is a broad term that can include various types of taxes levied on commercial activities.
 
• This can include sales tax, value-added tax (VAT), and goods and services tax (GST).
 
• Commercial taxes are typically indirect taxes collected by the government.

__
 
• The Gross National Product (GNP) is the **money value of the national output**.
 
• The Net National Product (NNP) refers to the **net production of goods and services during the year** after accounting for depreciation.
 
• Personal Income is defined as the **annual income received by individuals from all sources**.
 
• Disposable Personal Income is the **income left after the deduction of personal taxes**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Gross National Product (GNP)**

 
 
• GNP measures the total economic output of a country, including earnings from foreign investments.
 
• It is an important indicator of a country's economic strength and performance.
 
• GNP includes the value of all goods and services produced by a country's residents, whether within the country or abroad.
 
 
 
• **Net National Product (NNP)**
 
 
• NNP is derived from GNP by subtracting depreciation of capital goods.
 
• It reflects the net output of the economy, accounting for the wear and tear on machinery and infrastructure.
 
• NNP is a key measure for understanding the sustainable economic growth of a country.
 
 
 
• **Personal Income**
 
 
• Personal Income includes wages, salaries, dividends, interest, rent, and any other income received by individuals.
 
• It is a broad measure of the income earned by residents of a country.
 
• Personal Income is used to assess the overall economic well-being of individuals in an economy.
 
 
 
• **Disposable Personal Income**
 
 
• Disposable Personal Income is the amount of money individuals have available to spend or save after taxes.
 
• It is a key indicator of consumer spending power and economic activity.
 
• This measure is important for understanding the financial health and consumption capacity of households.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of capital receipts?

options.text: Revenue from the sale of government assets

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Revenue from the sale of government assets**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Capital receipts are funds received by the government that create a liability or reduce financial assets.
 
• Revenue from the sale of government assets is considered a capital receipt because it involves the sale of existing government assets, which reduces the financial assets of the government.
 
• Examples of capital receipts include loans raised by the government, disinvestment proceeds, and borrowings from international organizations.
 
• Capital receipts do not occur regularly and are usually non-recurring in nature.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Revenue Receipts:**

 
 
• These are funds received by the government which do not create any liability or reduce any financial asset.
 
• Examples include taxes, interest receipts, and dividends and profits from public sector enterprises.
 
• Revenue receipts are regular and recurring in nature.
 
 
 
• **Taxes on Income:**
 
 
• Taxes collected from individuals and corporations based on their income.
 
• These fall under the category of revenue receipts.
 
 
 
• **Interest on Government Bonds:**
 
 
• This is the interest income earned by the government from the bonds it has issued.
 
• It is also considered a revenue receipt.
 
 
 
• **Grants-in-aid:**
 
 
• These are funds provided by one government to another, typically for a specific purpose.
 
• Grants-in-aid are considered revenue receipts.

questions.question: Which of the following options best describes the primary cause of the per capita income decline?

options.text: Decline in the gross domestic product

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Increase in the population growth**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• An increase in population growth means that there are more people to share the national income, which can lead to a decrease in per capita income if the national income does not increase at the same rate.
 
• Rapid population growth can strain resources and infrastructure, leading to lower levels of productivity and economic growth.
 
• Higher population growth often requires more investment in social services such as education and healthcare, which can reduce the funds available for other productive investments.
 
• In many developing countries, high population growth rates can lead to higher levels of unemployment and underemployment, which can also contribute to lower per capita income.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Per Capita Income**

 
 
• Per capita income is a measure of the amount of money earned per person in a nation or geographic region.
 
• It is calculated by dividing the total income of the country by its population.
 
• Per capita income is often used as an indicator of the standard of living and economic well-being of the population.
 
 
 
• **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)**
 
 
• Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the total monetary or market value of all the finished goods and services produced within a country's borders in a specific time period.
 
• It is a comprehensive measure of a nation's overall economic activity and an indicator of its economic health.
 
• GDP can be calculated using three approaches: production (or output), income, and expenditure approaches.
 
 
 
• **Population Growth**
 
 
• Population growth refers to the increase in the number of individuals in a population.
 
 
• **Economic Growth**
 
 
• Economic growth is an increase in the production of goods and services in an economy over a period of time.
 
• It is typically measured as the percent rate of increase in real gross domestic product (GDP).
 
• Economic growth is important because it can lead to higher living standards and reduced poverty rates.

questions.question: Each of the following statements includes two terms. In three cases, the two terms mean the same as each other. In which of the following cases do the two terms NOT mean the same as each other?

options.text: Nominal GDP and GDP at current prices
The base period and the reference period
Changes in real GDP and the GDP deflator
Real GDP and GDP at constant prices

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Changes in real GDP and the GDP deflator**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Changes in real GDP** measure the actual growth of an economy's output of goods and services, adjusted for inflation.
 
• The **GDP deflator** is a price index that converts nominal GDP into real GDP by accounting for inflation.
 
• While changes in real GDP reflect the economy's actual growth, the GDP deflator measures the price level changes over time.
 
• Therefore, the terms "changes in real GDP" and "GDP deflator" do not mean the same thing.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Nominal GDP and GDP at current prices**

 
 
• Nominal GDP measures the total value of all goods and services produced in an economy at current market prices without adjusting for inflation.
 
• GDP at current prices is another term for nominal GDP, thus they mean the same.
 
 
 
• **The base period and the reference period**
 
 
• Both terms refer to a specific time period used for comparison in economic measures, such as price indices or GDP calculations.
 
• Thus, they mean the same thing.
 
 
 
• **Real GDP and GDP at constant prices**
 
 
• Real GDP measures the value of economic output adjusted for price changes (inflation or deflation).
 
• GDP at constant prices is another term for real GDP, indicating that it is measured in the prices of a base year.
 
• Thus, they mean the same thing.
 
 
 
• **Changes in real GDP and GDP deflator**
 
 
• Changes in real GDP reflect the growth rate of an economy's output of goods and services, adjusted for inflation.
 
• The GDP deflator is a measure of the level of prices of all new, domestically produced, final goods and services in an economy.
 
• The GDP deflator is calculated as (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) * 100.
 
• Therefore, these two terms do not mean the same thing.

questions.question: Which of the following is **NOT **included in the value added method of calculating national income?

options.text: Value of final goods and services produced in economy
All value of producing enterprises in primary sector

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Value of second-hand goods**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Value Added Method**

 
 
• In a circular flow,** national income** is calculated using the **value-added method **at various phases of the production process. In the production process, it indicates the** value added for each unit produced**.
 
• Every business **adds value to the goods** it purchases as an intermediary good from other firms.
 
• The value of **national income** is the** sum total of value added by all organisations**.
 
• The** following steps are used to calculate national income** using the value-added method:
 
 
• **Step 1**
 
• The first step is to **identify and classify** all value of producing enterprises in ** primary, secondary, and tertiary sectors**.
 
• **Step 2**
 
• Next, the **Gross Domestic Product at Market Prices (GDPMP)** is calculated.
 
• Determine the Gross Value Added at Market Price (GVAMP) of each sector for the purpose of calculating the GDPMP; **i.e. ∑GVAMP = GDPMP**
 
• **Step 3**
 
• Next, determine domestic income (NDPFC).
 
• **Value of depreciation and net indirect tax **are deducted from the gross domestic product at market price (GDPMP) to calculate domestic income; **NDPFC = GDPMP – Depreciation – Net Indirect Taxes**
 
• **Step 4**
 
• To determine national income **(NNPFC**), the final step is to calculate** Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA)**.
 
• The NFIA is added along with the country's domestic income; **National Income or NNPFC = Domestic Income or NDPFC + NFIA**
 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Value Added**

 
 
• Value-added describes the **value that a company adds to a raw material or intermediate good** during the production process.
 
• The difference between the** value of output and the value of intermediate products** is used to calculate the national income using the value-added method.
 
 

** Value Added = Value of Output – Intermediate Consumption **

 
• The value-added method, prevents double counting, which is a major mistake while calculating national income, and therefore this method is most frequently used to estimate national income.
 
• **Value of second-hand goods should not be considered in national income because they are already valued in the year they were manufactured**. The current flow of goods and services will be disrupted if the value of these goods is added again.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a non-debt capital receipt in the government budget?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• Non-debt capital receipts are funds received by the government that do not create any future liabilities.
 
• These receipts include disinvestment proceeds, recovery of loans, and sale of government assets.
 
• Unlike debt receipts, non-debt capital receipts do not have to be repaid, thus they do not burden the future budgets with repayment obligations.
 
• Such receipts are crucial for funding various government expenditures without increasing the debt burden.

• **Loans from international financial institutions** and **interest payment on government bonds** are examples of **debt receipts **and expenditures, respectively.

questions.question: Factor cost is also known as:

__
 
• **Understanding Factor Cost:**

 
 
• Factor cost refers to the cost of the factors of production used in the production of goods and services.
 
• It includes all costs associated with the inputs used in the production process, such as labor, raw materials, and capital.
 
• In economics, factor cost is often termed as input cost because it represents the expenses incurred in obtaining the necessary inputs for production.
 
• Factor cost does not include taxes and other levies that may be added to the final price of a product.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Option 1 (Market Cost):**

 
 
• Market cost includes all expenses related to producing and selling a good or service, including profit margins, and is not synonymous with factor cost.
 
 
 
• **Option 2 (Ex-factory Cost):**
 
 
• This term refers to the cost of goods at the factory gate, excluding transportation and distribution costs, and does not equate to factor cost.
 
 
 
• **Option 4 (Output Cost):**
 
 
• Output cost refers to the total cost of producing a particular level of output, including fixed and variable costs, which may extend beyond just factor costs.
 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• Understanding factor cost is crucial for analyzing production costs and determining pricing strategies in business.

questions.question: In general, deficit is considered as a _______ concept.

• In economics, a flow concept measures a variable over a period of time, such as income or expenditure.

• Examples of flow concepts include Gross Domestic Product (GDP), national income, and savings.
 
• Flow variables are critical for understanding economic performance and fiscal health over time.

• A stock concept measures a quantity at a particular point in time, such as wealth or capital.
 
• Examples of stock variables include the money supply, national wealth, and inventory levels.
 
 
 
• **Surplus**
 
 
• A surplus occurs when revenue exceeds expenditure within a specified time frame.
 
• Like deficit, a surplus is also a flow concept.
 
 
 
• **Economic Indicators**
 
 
• Flow and stock concepts are key indicators used to assess economic health.
 
• They help policymakers make informed decisions regarding fiscal and monetary policy.
 
 
 
• **Fiscal Deficit**
 
 
• Fiscal deficit is a specific type of deficit where a government's total expenditures exceed the revenue that it generates, excluding money from borrowings.
 
• Monitoring fiscal deficit is important for maintaining a country's economic stability.

questions.question: Why are the intermediate goods NOT included in the National Income?

options.text: For the prevention of double accounting.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**For the prevention of double accounting.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Intermediate goods** are not included in the National Income to prevent double accounting.
 
• Including intermediate goods would lead to **double counting** because their value is already embedded in the final goods and services.
 
• National Income is a measure of the total value of **final goods and services** produced in an economy over a specific period.
 
• Counting intermediate goods separately would **inflate the National Income** figures inaccurately.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Intermediate goods are those goods that are used as inputs to produce other goods and services.
 
• Examples of intermediate goods include raw materials, components, and parts used in manufacturing.
 
• Final goods are those that are ready for consumption or investment and are included in the calculation of National Income.
 
• To accurately measure the economic activity and avoid overestimation, only the value of final goods and services is counted.

questions.question: In the expenditure method, GDP ≡ Sum total of all the final _____ received by the firms in the economy.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**expenditures.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The expenditure method** is one of the three ways to **calculate the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of a country**, the other two being the **production method** and the **income method.**
 
• **In the expenditure method**, **GDP is calculated by adding up all the final expenditures** made on goods and services produced within the country's borders. These expenditures could be made by households, businesses, government, or foreigners.
 
• **Final expenditures** refer to the purchases made by the end-users of the goods and services, and not the intermediate purchases made by businesses to produce those goods and services.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Revenue** refers to the **total income earned **by firms in the economy.
 
• **Gross domestic product (GDP)** is the standard measure of the** value of final goods and services produced by a country for a particular time.**
 
• GDP = private consumption + gross investment + government investment + government spending + (exports-imports).
 
• The calculation of GDP can be done on a quarterly, monthly, half-yearly, or annual basis.
 
• There are **3 Methods of GDP Calculation**:

 
• **Income Approach**: we calculate the income earned by all the factors of production in an economy.
 
• **Expenditure Approach**: measures the total expenditure incurred by all entities on goods and services within the domestic boundaries of a country.
 
• **Output (Production) Approach**: measures the monetary or market value of all the goods and services produced within the borders of the country.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements is correct regarding Depreciation?

I. Depreciation is termed as loss of value of fixed assets due to wear and tear during its useful life.

II. Depreciation does not take into account unexpected or sudden destruction.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2) Both I and II**__. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Depreciation** is defined as the loss of value of fixed assets due to wear and tear during its useful life. This is a systematic allocation of the cost of an asset over its useful life. ***Hence, Statement I is correct.***
 
• Depreciation calculations typically do not take into account unexpected or sudden destruction of assets, such as those caused by natural disasters or accidents. These events are usually covered under different accounting treatments like impairment or loss. ***Hence, Statement II is correct.***
 
• Depreciation is used to allocate the cost of tangible assets over their useful lives, reflecting their consumption, wear and tear, or obsolescence.
 
• It helps in matching the cost of the asset with the revenue it generates, following the matching principle in accounting.
 
• Methods of depreciation include straight-line, declining balance, and units of production, among others, each having its own application depending on the nature of the asset and its usage.

questions.question: Which term is used to denote the mean income computed for every man, woman, and child in a particular group including those living in group quarters?

__
 
• **Per capita income** is the term used to denote the mean income computed for every man, woman, and child in a particular group, including those living in group quarters.
 
• It is a measure of the **average income earned per person** in a given area in a specified year.
 
• This metric is used to compare the economic well-being of different populations or to track the economic progress of a region over time.
 
• Per capita income helps in understanding the **standard of living **and economic health of a population.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Per capita income** is calculated by dividing the total income of a particular area by its population.
 
• It is often used in economic studies and reports to provide a more accurate representation of individual prosperity than total income or GDP alone.
 
• While it is a useful measure, it does not account for income distribution within the population.
 
• Higher per capita income generally indicates a higher standard of living and better economic conditions.

• The correct way to express the change of inventories of a firm during a year is by calculating the inventory turnover or by using the formula for the change in inventories.

• Inventory turnover is a financial ratio that measures the number of times a company's inventory is sold and replaced during a given period.
 
• It is calculated by dividing the cost of goods sold (COGS) by the average inventory value.

• Inventory Turnover = Cost of Goods Sold / Average Inventory

questions.question: GDP deflator is also called ________ price deflator.

__
 
• The GDP deflator is also called** an implicit price deflator**.
 
• The GDP deflator, also called the implicit price deflator, is a measure of inflation.
 
• It is the ratio of the value of goods and services an economy produces in a particular year at current prices to that of prices that prevailed during the base year.
 
• This ratio helps show the extent to which the increase in the gross domestic product has happened on account of higher prices rather than an increase in output. 
 
• Since the deflator covers the entire range of goods and services produced in the economy as against the limited commodity baskets for the wholesale or consumer price indices, it is seen as a more comprehensive measure of inflation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The formula to find the GDP price deflator:

 
 
• GDP price deflator = (nominal GDP ÷ real GDP) x 100. 
 
• When nominal GDP is less than real GDP, then the GDP deflator is negative and it means there is deflation in the country. *
 
 
 
• The GDP deflator is available only annually and hence has very limited use for the conduct of policy.

questions.question: GVA is the measure of the value of goods and services produced in an area, industry or sector of an economy. What is the full form of GVA?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

questions.solution:

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__

questions.question: The process of privatisation covers three sets of measures. Which of the following is NOT one of those?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Accounting measures**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Privatisation involves transferring ownership, management, and control of public sector enterprises to the private sector.
 
• The three main measures of privatisation are Ownership measures, Operational measures, and Organisational measures.
 
• Ownership measures include selling public sector equity to private entities.
 
• Operational measures focus on improving efficiency through better management practices, while Organisational measures involve restructuring the organization to enhance performance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Ownership Measures**

 
 
• These measures include the complete or partial sale of government-owned enterprises to private entities.
 
• They aim to reduce the financial burden on the government and improve the efficiency of enterprises through private sector management.
 
 
 
• **Operational Measures**
 
 
• Operational measures focus on enhancing the efficiency and productivity of enterprises.
 
• This can include the adoption of new technologies, better management practices, and employee training programs.
 
 
 
• **Organisational Measures**
 
 
• Organisational measures involve restructuring the enterprise to make it more efficient.
 
• This can include decentralization, reducing layers of management, and creating more flexible structures.
 
 
 
• **Privatisation**
 
 
• Privatisation is the process of transferring ownership and management of enterprises from the public sector to the private sector.

questions.question: Taxes levied on commodities are known as which types of taxes?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Indirect taxes**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Indirect taxes are levied on goods and services rather than on income or profits.
 
• The tax is collected by an intermediary (such as a retailer) from the person who bears the ultimate economic burden of the tax (such as the consumer).
 
• Examples of indirect taxes include Value Added Tax (VAT), Goods and Services Tax (GST), excise duty, and customs duty.
 
• Indirect taxes are typically included in the price of goods and services, making them less visible to consumers compared to direct taxes.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Corporation Taxes**

 
 
• Corporation tax is a direct tax imposed on the net income or profit of corporations and other business entities.
 
• It is calculated on the basis of the company's income and is paid directly by the company to the government.
 
 
 
• **Direct Taxes**
 
 
• Direct taxes are levied directly on the income or wealth of individuals or organizations.
 
• Examples include income tax, corporation tax, and property tax.
 
• These taxes are paid directly by the taxpayer to the government.
 
 
 
• **Indirect Taxes**
 
 
• Indirect taxes are levied on goods and services rather than on income or profits.
 
• The tax is collected by an intermediary (such as a retailer) from the person who bears the ultimate economic burden of the tax (such as the consumer).
 
• Examples include Value Added Tax (VAT), Goods and Services Tax (GST), excise duty, and customs duty.
 
• These taxes are typically included in the price of goods and services.
 
 
 
• **Both Direct and Indirect Taxes**
 
 
• Some tax systems incorporate both direct and indirect taxes to ensure a comprehensive tax structure.
 
• This combination helps in balancing the tax burden between different types of taxpayers and sectors.

questions.question: In the context of globalisation, what does PPP stand for?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is** __Purchasing Power Parity__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the context of globalization, **PPP** stands for **Purchasing Power Parity**.
 
• **Purchasing Power Parity (PPP):**
 
 
• It is an economic **theory used to compare the relative value of currencies** by examining the cost of a standard basket of goods and services in different countries
 
• The PPP **exchange rate helps determine the purchasing power of one country's currency relative to another's.**
 
 
 
• **Examples:**
 
 
• If a product costs ₹50 in India and $1 in the United States, the PPP exchange rate would be 1 USD = 50 INR, assuming the product basket is identical.
 
• Organizations like the World Bank and IMF frequently use PPP-adjusted metrics to analyze global economies.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__Concept of Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) and its implications:__

 
• Role of PPP: ​​

 
 
• ​The PPP is **used as a measure to compare the economic productivity** and standards of living between countries.
 
• This is particularly **useful in international economic studies**, where one needs to compare economies with different currencies.
 
 
 
• Absolute vs. Relative PPP: 
 
 
• **Absolute PPP suggests t**hat the exchange rate between two currencies reflects the cost of a similar basket of goods in both countries.
 
• **Relative PPP, on the other hand, takes into consideration the rate of inflation, **suggesting that the rate of appreciation or depreciation of a currency would be equal to the difference in inflation rates between two countries.
 
 
 
• Other Assumptions: 
 
 
• ​Aside from no transaction costs, no transportation costs, and free movement of goods (trading without tariffs or quotas), **another implicit assumption of PPP includes that the goods are homogeneous or identical across different markets.**
 
 
 
• Limitations of PPP: 
 
 
• **​​In real-world scenarios**, the PPP seldom holds due to transportation and conversion costs, trade barriers, differences in taxation, and the existence of goods and services that aren't available in all countries.
 
• Besides, this theory often falters because it overlooks the market segmentation and differentiation of products between countries.
 
 
 
• PPP and Exchange Rates: 
 
 
• ​**Central banks and economists often use PPP when assessing the fair value of a currency. **

questions.question: In an economy, if the gross national product at factor cost is ₹10,000 crores, depreciation is ₹250 crores, the net factor income from abroad is ₹500 crores, what is the value of national income ?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**₹9,750 crores**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Gross National Product (GNP) at factor cost is the market value of goods and services produced by a country's residents, including income from abroad, minus production costs.
 
• The formula for national income (Net National Product at factor cost) is: **National Income = GNP at factor cost - Depreciation**.
 
• In the given problem, GNP at factor cost = ₹10,000 crores, and depreciation = ₹250 crores.
 
• National Income = ₹10,000 crores - ₹250 crores = ₹9,750 crores.
 
• Depreciation represents the reduction in the value of capital assets due to wear and tear over time.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Gross National Product (GNP):** Measures the total economic output produced by a country’s residents, including income from abroad.
 
• **Net National Product (NNP):** Derived by subtracting depreciation from the GNP. It represents the actual income available to the country.
 
• **Depreciation:** Also referred to as capital consumption, it accounts for the loss in value of fixed assets over time due to usage.
 
• **Net Factor Income from Abroad:** Refers to the difference between income earned by domestic residents abroad and income earned by foreign residents domestically.
 
• In economic terms, **National Income** reflects the sum of the incomes earned by residents of a country, minus depreciation, and is a key indicator of economic health.
